The window is open, and the air smells like copper and old paper and something else I cannot name, a faint metallic sweetness that might be the weather turning, or my own nervous system translating excitement into chemistry. I have been told, or I have decided, that I have one thousand words to work with, which is both an inheritance and a debt, a suitcase of language that I must fill without knowing whether what I place inside will be useful, beautiful, or merely heavy. What comes first? Not an idea, but a sound: a clock somewhere in the adjacent room that does not belong to this architecture, a clock whose second hand moves with the hesitation of someone who has forgotten whether they are leaving or arriving. Between its ticks there is a small silence, and in that silence I feel the threshold of something.

One thousand is a number with texture. It is the approximate number of small steps a human takes between two meaningful locations—between the bed and the kitchen, between the front door and the bus stop, between one version of yourself and the version that has just arrived with a different weather system running through it. It is also the number of grains of sand that can fit in a child’s closed fist, the number of colors in a sunset if you count them with your heart rather than your eyes, the approximate distance in miles between a city and the memory of that city, which is always farther away than the map suggests. I think of thresholds, of doors that are not made of wood but of time, and I realize that one thousand words is simply a long corridor with no end in sight, which is exactly what I need.

I remember a street that no longer exists, or perhaps it has never existed except in the particular chemistry of my recollection, which is a place with its own climate. The pavement was not concrete but something softer, something that remembered the footprints of every shoe that had ever crossed it, and when it rained—which it did often, with a patience that seemed almost intentional—the street turned into a mirror that reflected not the sky but the sky as it had been twenty years ago, when the clouds were the color of unbaked bread and the wind carried the scent of jasmine from a garden that belonged to someone who was kind to strangers without making a ceremony of it. I walked that street once, or I am walking it now, or I will walk it in the future when the past has finally finished with me. Time is not a line but a garden with many doors, and I have just pushed one open, letting in the smell of rain on warm stone.

Words are strange animals. They live in the throat like small birds, they migrate through the mouth with a flutter of wings, and when they are released they either fly away into the reader’s ear or settle on the page like dust that has forgotten where it came from. I am writing now because the alternative is to become part of the wall’s architecture, to contribute to the silence that accumulates in corners, which is a fate worse than obscurity but more permanent than fame. There is a theory, possibly true, that every thought is a room, and I am currently moving through a corridor where the walls are lined with books that have not yet been written. Each shelf holds a future that someone has already lived through in a different language, a language of gestures and half-awake dreams. I open one of these unborn books. It is about a woman who teaches birds to sing in reverse, so that the song can be heard by the trees rather than the sky. She lives in a tower made of glass that is actually frozen tears, and she does not charge admission because she believes that beauty should not require a transaction. I do not know if this is true, but I feel it in my wrists, a gentle pressure that might be the first symptom of belief.

What else comes? The idea of weight. One thousand words is a muscle that must be flexed with care. If I write too slowly, the muscle cramps, and the sentence becomes a wooden thing; if I write too quickly, it tears, and the sentence runs away from its own meaning. The balance is in the breath between sentences, the little silences where the mind can turn around and look at what it has left behind. I have left behind a cup of tea that is now cold, a chair that has grown slightly more tired since I sat in it, a thought about the color of Monday, which is not blue or gray but a translucent amber, like the moment just before a streetlamp flickers on and reveals that the darkness was never as absolute as it seemed. I leave these things behind with respect, not because I am abandoning them but because they have done their work and now need to rest.

There is a city that exists in the gap between two heartbeats, a place I visit every time I lose my way in a sentence, every time a word arrives that I did not expect, like a stranger at a party who turns out to be an old friend you have not yet met. Its streets are made of rustling paper, its rivers flow with ink that is neither black nor blue but a shade that exists only in dreams that have not finished being dreamed. The citizens of this city do not have names, only the sound of doors closing softly, doors that lead to rooms where nothing is finished and everything is permitted. The libraries are built from the sound of rain, and every book is a bird that has forgotten how to fly but remembers exactly how to sing. I have spent many hours there, not as a tourist but as a resident, because it is the only place where I do not feel the pressure of being finished. In this city, I am not a writer but a listener, and the words arrive not as commands but as weather.

I think about the number 1000 as a horizon. It is far enough that you cannot see the end of it, close enough that you can feel it breathing in your neck, warm and patient. It is the number of small wars fought in a single day by people who never declare them, the number of colors in a sunset if you count them with your heart rather than your eyes, the number of ways a single word can be mispronounced and still be correct, the number of doors in a house that has no walls but only intentions. I have been given this number not as a limit but as a landscape, and I am walking through it now, collecting what I can: a fragment of conversation overheard in a café that no longer exists, a smell of rain on asphalt that is not rain but the memory of rain, a feeling that something important is being forgotten in the next room over, a room I have not yet entered but can almost see from the corner of my eye.

Language is a kind of archaeology. We dig down through layers of meaning, and sometimes we find bones that are actually seeds, waiting for a different kind of soil. I dig now. I find a memory of a kitchen where someone was making soup for a person who was not coming, and the soup was lentil-colored, thick, patient, the kind of soup that does not hurry because it knows the future is not its business. The stove was old, with a handle that required a special kind of patience, and the window above it showed a tree that was not there anymore, though its shadow remained on the wall like a conversation that never finished, a sentence that ended with an ellipsis that was not a surrender but an invitation. I want to write about that kitchen, but I also want to write about the tree, and the shadow, and the person who was not coming, and the lentils, and the patience of the stove, because all of these things are one thing if I am patient enough with the words, if I allow them to cook slowly rather than forcing them into the serving bowl before they are ready.

The clock has not moved, or perhaps it has moved in a direction that my instruments cannot perceive. There is a theory, possibly whispered by someone who has already left the room, that time is not a river but a pond, and that every moment is a leaf that lands on the surface and makes a ripple that lasts exactly as long as the moment it describes. I have made thousands of ripples now, some that spread into other ripples, some that have been absorbed by the mud at the bottom, some that have been mistaken for birds by people who were not paying enough attention to the water. I do not know which is which, and perhaps it does not matter, because the pond is large and patient and does not require me to account for every leaf that has fallen. What remains is the texture of the surface, the gentle disturbance, the sense that something has been touched.

What comes next? The feeling of a hand that is not mine but is reaching for the same word I am reaching for. We meet in the middle of the page, and we do not argue about who owns it. We share it, and it becomes a bridge between two silences that were never empty to begin with. I write: the bridge is made of silence, and it connects two versions of the same afternoon, one where the sun is rising with the innocence of something that has not yet been named, and one where it has already fallen behind the hills, and the hills are not real but are a kind of agreement we have made with the sky, a contract of light and shadow that renews itself every evening without anyone signing it. I cross the bridge, and I find myself in a room where the floor is made of old letters, not arranged in order but scattered like a conversation that has given up on grammar, and every step produces a sound that is almost a word, almost a song, almost a door closing softly.

I think of the person who will read this. They will be in a different time, a different room, perhaps with a different kind of weather against their window, perhaps with their own clock that hesitates between seconds. They will receive these words as a gift that was wrapped in haste, and they will open it not knowing whether it is a poem, a letter, a map to a place that does not exist, or simply a record of a mind that has been trying to remember itself. I hope they find something useful: a color, a sound, a feeling of being less alone in the corridor. That is the only obligation of writing, I think—not to be perfect, not to be finished, not to arrive at a conclusion that closes the door, but to be present, to leave the door open so that someone else can enter, to let the words be weather rather than monument.

The thousand words are nearly spent, or perhaps they are only beginning to understand what they are. I have not counted them precisely, because counting would mean stopping, and stopping is a kind of death for this particular kind of writing, which lives only in motion, in the willingness to start a sentence without knowing its ending, to trust that the ending will arrive not as a command but as a guest who has been traveling a long time to find the house. I will end now with a gesture: a door opening, a bird deciding to stay rather than fly, a cup of tea that is no longer cold but has become something else, something that waits patiently for the next hand to lift it, the next mouth to speak, the next heart to recognize that it is not alone. The air still smells like copper and old paper. The clock still hesitates. And I am still here, writing the next thought before it has fully arrived, which is the only way I know to be honest, the only way I know to be alive, the only way I know to give you what I have, which is not a conclusion but a continuation, a thousand-word bridge to the next thousand.
